## What Has Actually Been Measured in Golfers {#sec-lay-ch24}

## A Concrete Picture

A courtroom separates what a witness saw from the explanation offered for it.
Golf science needs the same separation. A marker trajectory, a calibrated grip
load, and an electrical signal from a muscle can constrain an explanation of the
swing. They do not carry the same information, and collecting them together does
not automatically reveal the internal mechanism.

The useful question is specific: what observation would distinguish two plausible
explanations? If both predict the same club motion but different hand loads,
another camera may add less information than a carefully calibrated grip
measurement. If both predict the same hand loads through different muscle
combinations, even a perfect grip sensor leaves a biological question open.

![Observations Constrain Inferences; Each Explanation Still Needs a Test.](figures/proximal_distal_companion/fig_companion_human_evidence_pyramid.svg){#fig-lay-human-evidence width=96% fig-alt="Four equal-width panels distinguish calibrated observations, mechanical inference, anatomical inference, and prospective tests. Additional measurements constrain explanations without guaranteeing a unique biological mechanism."}

## How the Mechanism Works

### Separate the Signal From the Explanation

A camera records image information from which marker positions and segment
motion are reconstructed. A force plate converts transducer signals into a
calibrated external wrench. A grip sensor records a load at its sensing section;
the force attributed to a palm can require a further mechanical calculation.
EMG records electrical activity associated with selected muscles, not muscle
force directly. Every measurement has a location, reference frame, bandwidth,
calibration, and uncertainty.

Inverse dynamics combines motion, external loads, and body-segment inertias to
estimate net joint loads. Its answer depends on filtering and differentiation,
joint definitions, and the assumed contact model. In the closed chain formed by
two arms and one club, the net club wrench alone generally does not identify how
the hands share the load. Additional sensing or assumptions are required.

Even uniquely determined net joint moments would not uniquely determine muscle
forces. Antagonists can increase their opposing forces while leaving a similar
net moment. EMG can constrain activation timing and a muscle model, but the
conversion to force also depends on muscle length, contraction velocity,
activation dynamics, and tendon behavior. Mechanical identification and
anatomical identification are different problems.

### A Bounded Register of Human Evidence

The following studies illustrate what the literature can constrain. They are a
selected register, not a new systematic search or a pooled dataset. Participant
counts refer to people, not independent replications of every recorded swing.
The linked sources identify the studies; unspecified trial counts or data access
should be checked in the full methods before reanalysis.

- **Kinematics Across Studies.** Bourgain and colleagues' systematic review
  included 92 studies and documented heterogeneous definitions and methods
  [@bourgain2022]. It supports careful comparison of coordinate systems, clubs,
  samples, and events; it does not establish one universal sequence. This is
  distinct from McPhee and colleagues' narrative model-and-measurement review
  [@mcphee2022].
- **Professional and Amateur Motion.** Zheng and colleagues compared 72 men,
  with 18 in each of four professional/amateur skill groups, using motion capture
  at 240 Hz [@zheng2008]. Group differences describe the sampled swings. They
  do not establish that copying a professional's movement causes improvement or
  prevents injury.
- **Scapular Muscle Activity.** Kao, Pink, Jobe, and Perry studied 15 competitive
  male golfers with bilateral EMG of four scapular muscles and cinematography
  [@kao1995]. Phase- and side-dependent activity supports shoulder-girdle
  involvement. It does not identify a unique route from a scapular muscle to a
  handle moment.
- **A Specific Wrist Muscle.** Robinson and colleagues studied bilateral
  extensor carpi ulnaris activity in 15 subelite, right-handed men, with five shots
  each using a pitching wedge, 7-iron, and driver [@robinson2023]. Surface EMG and
  forearm/hand inertial sensors characterized selected activation and movement
  variables. These are not measurements of all wrist muscles. The reported
  nonsignificant downswing-EMG association with impact clubhead kinematics does
  not establish no effect or equivalence.
- **A Strain-Gauge Handle.** Koike and colleagues demonstrated reconstructed
  palm forces and moments for one right-handed professional instructor using a
  driver [@koike2016instrumented]. Their calibration and mechanical calculation
  use fixed palm reference points and neglect handle-piece inertia. This is a
  useful instrument demonstration, not population validation or direct muscle
  measurement.
- **A Split Grip and Inverse Dynamics.** Choi and Park studied nine right-handed
  male professionals with five regular-grip driver swings followed by five
  instrumented-grip swings [@koike2020]. One six-axis sensor between two grip
  sections supplied an internal wrench; a nine-segment rigid-body model inferred
  hand and upper-limb joint loads. Separate hand loads are therefore estimates
  supported by sensing and a model, not two independent raw sensor outputs.
- **Ground Interaction.** Han and colleagues studied 63 skilled male golfers
  with handicaps at most three, using driver, 5-iron, and pitching-wedge shots,
  optical motion capture, and two force plates [@han2019]. They computed
  ground-interaction moments and found associations with clubhead speed. Those
  associations do not identify a unique ground-to-club energy pathway.
- **Shaft Stiffness.** Betzler and colleagues studied 20 golfers with two clubs
  designed to differ only in shaft bending stiffness [@betzler2012]. Their
  examination of shaft strain, wrist motion, club presentation, and ball launch
  found small speed differences for the tested shafts. This bounds a specific
  equipment comparison; it does not establish that shaft flexibility is always
  negligible or that one stiffness suits everyone.

### Why Instrument Design Changes the Claim

The Choi--Park instrumented grip weighed about 350 g versus about 100 g for a
regular grip; the instrumented club weighed 551 g. Foam/sponge balls, possible
hand-to-hand load bypass, and regular-club-first ordering further limit the
comparison. Similar average trajectories do not prove unchanged muscle control
or mechanical equivalence. The reported roughly threefold right-hand torque
relative to the left is a model-derived result in this setting, not a universal
hand contribution or muscle-power ratio [@koike2020].

The central lesson is constructive: record what the instrument closes in the
mechanical accounting and what remains assumed. A six-component signal at one
section is not automatically a six-component contact wrench at each hand. Loads
must be expressed about declared points in compatible frames. Acceleration of
material between sensor and contact introduces inertial terms; a path that
bypasses the sensor can carry an unrecorded internal load. Static calibration
alone does not establish dynamic accuracy over the swing's frequency range.

### Motion, Ground, Hands, and Shaft Belong in One Test

Kinematic peak order is a description of motion. It does not uniquely reveal
intersegmental energy transfer, and changing the angular-velocity component or
event definition can change the reported sequence [@bourgain2022; @marsan2019].
Likewise, a large ground force is not itself a large supply of mechanical work:
an ideal stationary contact can exchange momentum while its contact power is
zero. The body's muscular work and stored energy must still be accounted for.

At the hands, power pairs a wrench with the corresponding linear and angular
velocity; work integrates that power over time. Force magnitude alone is
insufficient. At the shaft, deformation can store and return energy
and alter clubhead presentation. A head-speed change can therefore accompany
changes in body motion, bilateral loading, shaft recovery, or several together.
Synchronized measurements let a model predict their joint pattern instead of
explaining one curve after the fact. They also require synchronized uncertainty:
a timing offset between force and velocity can corrupt a computed power curve.

The EMG result supplies another constraint, not a shortcut around this accounting.
Different activation patterns can produce similar net wrenches; similar EMG
amplitudes can accompany different forces under different muscle states.
Crosstalk, electrode placement, normalization, and limited sampling matter. A
nonsignificant association leaves an uncertainty interval to examine; an
equivalence claim needs a justified equivalence margin and an appropriate test.

### Repeated Swings and Independent Golfers

Extra swings help estimate a person's repeatability. Extra participants address
variation between people. These contributions should not be confused when
estimating a population mean or comparing groups. Nested observations require
an analysis that accounts for their dependence, such as an appropriate mixed
model or participant-level summaries [@lazic2010].

Consider a **manufactured example**, not measured golfer data. Let $y_{ij}$ be a
scalar outcome on swing $j$ from person $i$. Write

$$
y_{ij}=\mu+b_i+e_{ij}.
$$

Here $\mu$ is the population mean, $b_i$ is a zero-mean person-specific offset
with variance $\sigma_b^2$, and $e_{ij}$ is zero-mean within-person variation
with variance $\sigma_e^2$. Assume independent participants, errors independent
of the offsets and of each other, equal trial counts $m$, and no additional
session or time dependence. For $N$ people and their grand mean $\bar y$,

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\bar y)
=\frac{\sigma_b^2}{N}+\frac{\sigma_e^2}{Nm}.
$$

The person offset repeats in every one of that person's swings, so its
contribution shrinks with the number of people, not the total number of swings.
With $N=15$, $m=10$, and both variances set to one in squared outcome units, the
variance of the grand mean is $11/150$. Falsely treating all 150 swings as independent gives
$2/150$: uncertainty variance is understated by a factor of 5.5. The corresponding
variance-equivalent independent-observation count is $300/11$, about 27.3. That
number is neither 27 independent people nor a universal degrees-of-freedom rule.

More repeats reduce the second variance term but cannot eliminate the first at
fixed $N$. If between-person variance is zero, the formula reduces to the
independent-observation case; if each person contributes one swing, there is no
repeated-measure inflation. Real analyses may need condition effects, random
slopes, unequal trial counts, session effects, or residual autocorrelation.
Sample-size calculations must target the actual contrast and dependence model;
these invented variances are not a golf-study power calculation.

### Prediction, Estimation, and Causation Need Different Designs

An analysis estimating a population association does not automatically need a
prediction holdout, but it does need an appropriate sampling and uncertainty
model. A claim about predicting a new golfer requires evaluation on participants
excluded from fitting and model selection, with preprocessing learned only from
training data. Randomly splitting swings can leak a person's characteristics
into both sets. A different target, such as predicting a new session for a known
golfer, calls for a different split.

Neither a hierarchical model nor successful prediction alone identifies a causal
mechanism. A causal claim must state the intervention or contrast, potential
confounders, and assumptions that distinguish rival explanations. A model fitted
to a mean curve has not passed a held-out test merely because it reproduces that
curve. Multiple tested outcomes and exploratory choices also require transparent
reporting; select the primary outcome and analysis before inspecting results.

### The Specific Gap in This Project

The evidence reviewed here does not provide this project with a single
synchronized human dataset that validates the complete proposed passive
negative-couple and preload pathway. That is a statement about the evidence
assembled for this mechanism, not a claim that no relevant human study exists
anywhere. Existing reviews provide context [@hume2005; @mcphee2022], but combining
results from different participants and instruments does not create a joint
validation experiment.

**Human Evidence:** Motion patterns, selected muscle activity, ground reactions,
grip measurements, and shaft behavior constrain parts of the explanation within
their study designs. **Model Result:** Simulations predict coupled changes in
hand loads, club motion, and timing under specified assumptions. **Hypothesis:**
The proposed complete biological pathway remains to be tested with measurements
and contrasts capable of separating it from alternatives.

For the full pathway, seek synchronized whole-body and club motion, separate foot
reactions, sufficiently resolved bilateral hand loading, shaft deformation,
selected forearm/shoulder/scapular EMG, and launch outcomes. Contact pressure can
help characterize grip location and distribution but does not replace a full
wrench. Not every smaller scientific question requires every channel; select
channels according to what distinguishes the competing predictions.

### Turn Disagreement Into a Diagnostic

Suppose a model predicts a negative hand couple in a specified interval, but the
estimated experimental couple is positive. First check sign conventions,
reference points, synchronization, and uncertainty. If the disagreement persists
beyond the prespecified tolerance under comparable conditions, that prediction
has failed. Retuning the model can produce a new hypothesis, but does not erase
the failed prospective test.

If hand loads agree while EMG timing differs, examine activation measurement and
the proposed anatomical allocation. Agreement in net mechanics need not validate
the muscle explanation. If motion agrees while hand or ground loads disagree,
the model fails that additional constraint; the discrepancy may come from
parameters, missing dynamics, or measurement error. It does not uniquely diagnose
one cause. Failure in one observable should remain visible alongside success in
another.

### A Reproducible Human-Evidence Release

Before testing predictions, specify calibration acceptance, synchronization
tolerance, coordinate registration, sensor range, residual checks, exclusions,
and missing-data treatment. Relate thresholds to the intended measurement and
claim; there is no universal residual limit that validates every model.
Freeze the model version and primary comparisons, and disclose later deviations.

Release the protocol, data dictionary, processing code, participant and trial
counts, uncertainty, and consent-compatible data. Show individual traces and
residuals alongside group summaries. Report raw-data availability explicitly;
open access to a paper does not imply that participant-level data are available.
Synthetic pipeline examples and digitized published curves must remain labeled
as such. Neither substitutes for a new human validation sample.

### Reader Lab: Follow One Claim Through the Chain

Take the sentence "elite golfers sequence segments proximally to distally."
Check which people, club, coordinate components, filters, and peak definitions
support it. Determine whether the pattern occurs within individuals or only in
an average. A kinematic description needs reliable motion measurements; a claim
that this sequence transfers energy needs additional kinetic and power evidence.

Now examine "scapular muscles create the handle torque." Phase-dependent EMG
supports selected muscle involvement. Attribution of a particular handle torque
requires a closed-chain mechanical and anatomical model constrained by more
measurements. Even then, check whether competing muscle allocations remain
possible. Write separate sentences for the observation, the model inference, and
the untested causal claim. This makes the next experiment's purpose concrete.

## Where the Picture Breaks

The courtroom analogy makes observations sound neutral. Markers move relative
to bone, electrical signals have artifacts, and force estimates depend on
calibration and modeling choices. A richer instrument package improves the
constraints only when its uncertainties and load paths are understood.

Small or specialized samples also limit generalization across sex, age, skill,
injury history, anatomy, and equipment. Evidence can strengthen a bounded
mechanism without becoming a universal technique. The goal is a connected test
of motion, contact, energy, and biological allocation whose successes and
failures are both available to the reader.
